summary: This standards-track document sets aside codepoint ranges in the PCEP registries for experimental use. PCEP is the protocol used to communicate with a Path Computation Element, and IANA keeps registries of its message, object and TLV types. Reserving experimental ranges lets people try new extensions without taking permanent values.

eli5.summary: A school keeps some blank name tags for visitors to try out. This sets aside blank numbers in a protocol so experiments do not clash with real ones.

questions: how to test new pcep extensions without iana allocation
which pcep message types are experimental
what pcep tlv range is for experimental use
what does pcep do with unknown experimental messages
subtitle: Reserving PCEP message, object and TLV numbers so experiments never collide with real ones.

tldr.problem: Researchers need numbers to test new PCEP functions, but the PCEP registries allocated everything by IETF Review, and early allocation is reserved for features considered appropriately stable.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8356 updates RFC 5440 so that the top of the message, object and TLV registries is marked Experimental Use: message types 252-255, object identifiers 248-255 and TLV types 65504-65535.
tldr.outcome: Experimenters have values that will not collide with existing codepoints or future allocations. They are not meant for general deployment, and two experiments sharing them must not run in the same environment.

today: RFC 8356 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2018. It updates RFC 5440, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Experiments Need Reserved Numbers
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP, RFC 5440) lets Path Computation Elements (PCEs) compute paths in response to Path Computation Client (PCC) requests. Stateful extensions in RFC 8231 and RFC 8281 added control of MPLS-TE and GMPLS LSPs.

IANA keeps a top-level registry of PCEP codepoints with sub-registries for message, object and TLV types, each allocated by IETF Review (RFC 8126). Early allocation (RFC 7120) gives some latitude but is reserved for features considered appropriately stable.

Rapid advancements in PCE technology created a greater need to experiment. Even in a closed environment a test needs some number or constant, and it must not collide with existing codepoints or future allocations.
sections.eli5: If you want to try a new game with made-up pieces, you need pieces that are not already used in the real game. This sets aside some spare ones.

sections.title: What Is Set Aside
sections.content:
This document updates RFC 5440 by changing the allocation policies of three registries, marking some codepoints as assigned for Experimental Use. As RFC 3692 states, experiments using these codepoints are not intended for general deployments, and due care must be taken that two experiments using the same codepoints are not run in the same environment.

  • Messages: types are in the range 0 to 255; types 252-255 are set aside.
  • Objects: identifiers are in the range 0 to 255; identifiers 248-255 are set aside.
  • TLVs: type codes are in the range 0 to 65535; codes 65504-65535 are set aside.
sections.eli5: The numbers at the very end of each list are now the "try-it-out" numbers. Everyone knows not to hand them out for real things.

sections.title: Handling Unknown Experiments
sections.content:
A PCEP implementation that receives an experimental message it does not recognize reacts by sending a PCErr message with Error-Type=2 (capability not supported), per Section 6.9 of RFC 5440.

For an unsupported experimental object, handling depends on the message type. A PCE handles an unknown object in a Path Computation Request (PCReq) message by the rules of RFC 5440, and message-specific behavior may be specified. For example, RFC 8231 defines rules for a PCC to handle an unknown object in a Path Computation LSP Update Request (PCUpd) message. As per Section 7.1 of RFC 5440, an unknown experimental TLV would be ignored.
sections.eli5: If someone gets a message from an experiment they do not know, they politely say "I cannot do that" for messages, or just skip an unknown extra label.

sections.title: The Registry Changes
sections.content:
IANA maintains the "Path Computation Element Protocol (PCEP) Numbers" registry. Its three sub-registries now read as follows.

  • "PCEP Messages": 0-251 IETF Review, 252-255 Experimental Use.
  • "PCEP Objects": 0-247 IETF Review, 248-255 Experimental Use. Object-Types 0-15 have also been marked for Experimental Use.
  • "PCEP TLV Type Indicators": 0-65503 IETF Review, 65504-65535 Experimental Use.

IANA has also marked the experimental values in each registry accordingly.
sections.eli5: The official list now has two parts: normal numbers handed out with review, and a block at the end kept for experiments.

sections.title: Security and Other Registries
sections.content:
The document introduces no new security considerations. RFC 3692 asserts that experimental codepoints introduce none, but implementations accepting them need to take care in parsing and processing messages, objects and TLVs in case they come, accidentally, from another experiment, and need to consider the security of the experimental extensions themselves. RFC 6709 gives design considerations for protocol extensions.

Appendix A explains why only these three registries received experimental ranges, based on feedback from the PCE working group: if an experiment wants a new codepoint in another sub-registry, it can implement the same function with a new experimental object or TLV instead.
sections.eli5: Because experiments can show up by accident, programs should be careful with unexpected experimental messages. Other lists did not need spare numbers, since an experiment can use a spare object or TLV instead.
